Under the HoodEmulator InternalsZX Spectrum Next: how the sound is madeThe big picture

The Big Picture: Four Sources, One Mixer

A 48K Spectrum had one bit of sound and a speaker the size of a coin. Play a modern game on a ZX Spectrum Next, and you hear chip music in nine voices, in stereo, with sampled drums and speech on top. And the same machine still loads a tape by listening to it. So where does each of those sounds come from, and how do they all end up in one pair of headphones?

Sound does a lot of work in a program. Music sets the mood and the pace of a game. An effect tells you that you jumped, fired or were hit before your eyes have found it on the screen. Speech and sampled sounds make a game feel larger than its 128K. On a Spectrum, sound had one more job, too: programs were saved to tape and loaded from it as sound. And a machine with several sound sources that run by themselves does all this without tying up the CPU, which is busy enough drawing the screen, thank you very much.

This is the map of the Next’s sound, the first of its sound chapters. The chapters that follow take each source apart; here you see how they fit together. If digital sound is new to you, read How a Computer Makes Sound first: it explains samples, the DAC, the filter that makes the result smooth, sound from a single bit and mixing, and I will not explain them again. ZX Spectrum: How the Screen Is Drawn explains port $FE, which the beeper shares with the border, and The ZX Spectrum Next Core and the FPGA explains why the Next’s hardware lives in an FPGA.

The road ahead

We start where the Spectrum started, with one bit, and see what the Next kept and what it added beside it: four kinds of source. Then the whole cast walks on stage in one figure, and you hear each source on its own, one by one. After that comes the idea I would ask you to keep if you keep only one: some sources make a sound by themselves, and others need the CPU at every step, and that difference decides what a sound costs your program. From there we follow the sound downstream, into the one mixer that adds everything on a left and a right side, and out through the jack, the speaker, HDMI and the Pi. Two clocks explain why the CPU’s speed changes the beeper’s pitch but not the AY’s, and a handful of registers turn each part on and off. We end with the chapters that follow, and with how Klive makes the same sound.

The numbers in the sound chapters are for the Next’s 28 MHz master clock, with the CPU at 3.5 MHz unless a chapter says otherwise. Levels are given in the units of the Next’s mixer, whose sum runs from 0 to 8,191 per side. The waveforms are captured from Klive’s emulated Next at 48,000 samples a second, from programs checked to do what the text says; they show Klive’s mix of the sound, which keeps the hardware’s proportions (How Klive does it, near the end, says how).

From one bit to four kinds of source

The ZX Spectrum 48K makes sound with one bit. Bit 4 of port $FE, called EAR, drives the speaker: the program sets it, clears it, sets it again, and the speaker’s cone follows. Bit 3, MIC, drives the tape output and reaches the same speaker more weakly. Every sound a 48K program makes, from a key click to two-voice music, is the program switching those bits on and off at the right moments. The speaker is driven in the program’s own time: while it plays, your program can do little else.

The Spectrum 128K added a sound chip, the AY-3-8910, with three voices that play by themselves once they are set up. The Next keeps both and adds more beside them:

That makes four kinds of source: the beeper, with its two bits EAR and MIC (MIC also carries the tape input), the AY chips, the DACs and the Pi. Everything that follows, here and in the chapters after this one, is about these four, the mixer that adds them, and the outputs the sum leaves through.

Notice what did not change. The Spectrum’s sound stays exactly as it was. A 48K program that toggles port $FE bit 4 hears the same square wave; a 128K tune that writes the AY through ports $FFFD and $BFFD plays on the first AY chip exactly as it did on the 128K. Everything new is switched off or out of the way until a program asks for it, as The switches, further down, shows.

The cast

Here is the whole system in one figure. The sources are on the left, each in the colour it keeps throughout the sound chapters, with the ports and registers your program uses to drive it:

Before we meet the sources one by one, let’s hear them. Each capture below is a program playing a tone of about 1,000 Hz through one source alone:

The level scale is the point of this figure: it shows how loud each source can be next to the others. A DAC or the Pi playing at full scale is about twice as loud as the beeper, and one AY channel is half as loud as the beeper.

Have you noticed that the four tones are all close to 1,000 Hz, but not equal? Each source gets its pitch from its own clock, divided by whole numbers the program chooses, and only some pitches come out of whole numbers:

  • The beeper: 3,500,000 ÷ (2 × 1,760) = 994 Hz. The CPU’s 3.5 MHz clock, divided by the length of the program’s loop in T-states, twice per cycle; the loop’s length can change only in steps of 13 T-states.
  • The AY channel: 218,750 ÷ (2 × 109) = 1,003 Hz. The chip’s counters, divided by the channel’s period; the next period, 110, gives 994 Hz.
  • The DAC: 3,500,000 ÷ (218 × 16) = 1,003 Hz. The CPU’s clock again, divided by the 218 T-states between two writes and the 16 writes of one cycle.
  • The Pi: exactly 1,000 Hz. The Pi sends samples it has already worked out for that pitch, so the Next only plays them back.

The clocks behind the sound, further down, explains where these clocks come from.

The beeper, EAR and MIC

The beeper is the 48K’s one bit, unchanged: port $FE bit 4. While the bit is 1, it adds 512 units to both sides of the mixer; while it is 0, nothing. Your program makes a note by switching it at the note’s pitch: the capture above is a loop that flips the bit every 1,760 T-states, which at 3.5 MHz is a square wave of 3,500,000 ÷ (2 × 1,760) = 994 Hz.

Port $FE bit 3, MIC, adds 128 units while it is 1: a quarter of EAR, the ratio the 48K’s resistors gave the two bits. On the Next, the MIC line is more than the port bit. Before it reaches the mixer, it is combined with the tape input, the signal arriving at the EAR socket from a tape recorder, and with an EAR bit the Pi’s audio can produce. So you hear a tape load at MIC’s level, as on the original machine. The same line goes out of the MIC socket, so a program saves to tape by switching bit 3.

The beeper costs the CPU all its time while it plays, and its pitch depends on how fast the CPU runs. The Beeper: EAR, MIC and the Tape explains the bits, the tape input and how one bit can play two voices.

Three AY chips

The Next has three copies of the 128K’s sound chip. Each has three channels, A, B and C, and each channel plays a square wave at a pitch set by a 12-bit period, mixed with noise if you want, at one of 16 fixed volumes or following an envelope, a shape that rises or falls by itself. A chip can behave as the original General Instrument AY-3-8910 or as Yamaha’s compatible YM2149, which has a finer envelope.

The 128K’s own ports reach them: port $FFFD selects a register, port $BFFD writes it. A special value written to port $FFFD (one with bit 7 set, which no register number has) selects which chip the following writes go to, and that is all your program needs to play nine channels. This is TurboSound Next. One full channel adds up to 255 units to the mixer, and with every channel of all three chips at full volume a side gets at most 2,295.

The capture above is chip 0’s channel B, with period 109: a square wave of 1,003 Hz, written once and left alone. One AY Chip: Tones, Noise and Envelopes takes a single chip apart, and TurboSound: Three AY Chips Behind Two Ports adds the other two, the stereo modes and panning.

Four 8-bit DACs

A DAC channel holds an 8-bit number the CPU writes, and adds it to the mixer until the next write. The Next has four, A and B on the left side and C and D on the right. Each side adds its two channels and multiplies them by 4: up to 2,040 units.

The Spectrum and Pentagon world had half a dozen sound cards built on such DACs (Soundrive, Covox, Specdrum and others), each on its own ports. The Next answers on all of their ports, so their software plays unchanged. It also adds three NextRegs, $2C to $2E, through which the Copper, or a program with no free port, can write them. The capture above is a sine wave, 16 steps per cycle, written to port $DF, Specdrum’s port, which writes channels A and D at once and so reaches both sides. The 8-Bit DACs: Four Channels, Six Sound Cards explains them in full.

The Raspberry Pi’s audio

Inside the Next sits a Raspberry Pi Zero, connected by, among other things, an I2S link: a connection of a few wires that carries a stream of digital samples, left and right, in both directions. The Pi can play anything a small Linux computer can (an MP3, a speech synthesiser, another computer’s sound chip in software) and send the result to the Next, which adds it to the mixer at 10 bits per side: up to 1,023 units.

The link also works the other way, sending the Next’s own sound to the Pi. And the Pi’s stream can be turned into the EAR bit of the tape input, so that the Next loads a program the Pi plays. The PI I2S Audio Control register, NextReg $A2, sets it all up. The capture above is a 1,000 Hz sine, streamed in. Audio from the Raspberry Pi: Samples on Four Wires explains the link.

Generators and level writers

The captures in The cast look alike, but they are made in two very different ways. Here is the idea I promised, and it decides what a sound costs your program:

  • A generator makes a waveform by itself from a few settings. The AY chips are generators: the program writes a period, a volume and which channels are on, and the chip plays that tone until it is told otherwise, for a second or for an hour, without any help from the CPU.
  • A level writer holds whatever level it was given last. The beeper and the DACs are level writers: they make a waveform only if the CPU (or the DMA, or the Copper) writes a new level at every step of it, on time.

Here are the same two captures, with the CPU’s writes marked under them:

The DAC’s sine costs 16 writes per cycle, 16,055 a second, each one on time. If a write comes late, the step comes late, and the wave is distorted. Your program can afford that for a drum hit or a word of speech, or it can hand the job to the DMA, which copies a sample to a DAC port at a fixed rate on its own (the DAC chapter shows how). The AY’s tone costs nothing while it plays. That is why games of the 128K era played their music on the AY: the program runs the game and touches the chip only when the tune moves to the next note, typically once every frame.

In return, a level writer can play anything: any recorded sound, any waveform the program can compute. A generator plays only what its counters can make: square waves, noise and envelope shapes. The Next has both kinds, so you choose per sound. Here is my advice: AY music, with DAC drums over it. The two get along splendidly.

One mixer, two sides

Every source ends in one place: the mixer, which adds them. It has two sides, and every source gives each side its own number. For the beeper the two numbers are always the same; the AY chips, the DACs and the Pi can make them differ, which is what places a sound left or right (the background chapter’s section Two speakers explains stereo).

On each side, the mixer adds five numbers, many million times a second. The beeper gives two of them, one for each of its bits, and every other source one:

  • EAR: 512 while port $FE bit 4 is 1, otherwise 0.
  • MIC: 128 while the MIC line is 1, otherwise 0.
  • The AY chips: 0 to 2,295, the three chips’ channels on that side added together.
  • The DACs: 0 to 2,040, that side’s two channels (each 0–255) added and multiplied by 4.
  • The Pi: 0 to 1,023, the side’s 10-bit sample.

The sum is a 13-bit number, 0 to 8,191. Here is how much of that range each source can take:

Two things in the figure deserve a closer look.

The sum always fits. Every source at its loudest adds up to 5,998, well below 8,191, so the sum itself never overflows. The audio jack is tighter: it takes only the sum’s lowest 12 bits, up to 4,095. That is plenty for loud music with the beeper on top, but not for every source at full scale at once. The mixer chapter’s Headroom shows how much room real mixes need, and what the jack does past 4,095.

Silence is not zero. Every input is a number from 0 upwards; nothing is ever subtracted. A DAC at rest holds $80, the middle of its range, so that a sample can swing both ways from it, and the two on each side add 1,024 units even when no program has touched them. The Pi’s rest level is the middle of its range too, 512. So a silent Next sits at 1,536, and every sound moves up and down around whatever constant level its sources add. Sounds alarming? It is not. The background chapter’s section on mixing explains why that does no harm: a capacitor after the converters removes any constant level before the sound reaches a speaker. The Mixer: One Sum, Three Outputs takes all of this apart.

Where the sound goes

The two sums leave the machine by four ways at once:

  • The audio jack gets each side’s lowest 12 bits through a one-bit converter: a single pin of the FPGA switched on and off at 28 MHz, more often “on” the larger the number, and a resistor and a capacitor on the board that smooth the pulses into a voltage. It is the converter the background chapter calls delta-sigma.
  • The internal speaker gets one mono signal, the left and right sums added together, through one more converter of the same kind. The Peripheral 3 Setting register, NextReg $08, bit 4 switches it on (and it is on after power-on). With bit 6 of the Peripheral 2 Setting register, NextReg $06, also set, the speaker plays only the beeper, and EAR and MIC leave the mix. So your program can click keys and beep alerts on the speaker without disturbing the music in the headphones.
  • HDMI audio sends the sums as numbers, 48,000 samples a second, each a 16-bit word, beside the picture on the HDMI cable. Bit 2 of the Peripheral 4 Setting register, NextReg $09, silences it.
  • The Raspberry Pi receives the sums over the I2S link, when the link is set up to send.

One line goes out separately: the MIC line, port $FE bit 3 combined with the tape input and the Pi’s EAR bit, drives the MIC socket, the tape recorder’s input. That is how a program saves to tape.

Well, here is a detail worth a second look: the jack and the speaker have no sample rate. Their converters follow the sum as it changes, 28 million times a second. Only HDMI samples it, because HDMI carries sound as numbers. The mixer chapter explains each output.

The clocks behind the sound

Every part of the Next runs from one master clock of 28 MHz. Two branches of it time the sound, and they behave differently when the CPU’s speed changes:

The AY chips’ clock is fixed. The master clock divided by 16 gives 1.75 MHz, close to the 1.77 MHz of the 128K’s AY, and each chip divides that by 8 again: its counters step 218,750 times a second. A tone’s pitch is that rate divided by twice the channel’s period. So period 109 gives 218,750 ÷ 218 = 1,003 Hz, and the A of 440 Hz needs a period of 249 (439.3 Hz, as close as a whole number allows). Neither the CPU’s speed nor anything else a program does changes these clocks, so AY music plays at the same pitch at 3.5 MHz and at 28 MHz.

The beeper and the DACs follow the CPU. They change only when an instruction writes them, so their timing is the program’s. A loop that flips port $FE bit 4 every 1,760 T-states makes 994 Hz at 3.5 MHz and twice that, 1,989 Hz, at 7 MHz. The Next’s CPU can run at 3.5, 7, 14 or 28 MHz (the CPU Speed register, NextReg $07), so a beeper tune written for the 48K plays an octave higher at 7 MHz, and a sample player plays its samples faster. Chipmunks, anyone?

Contention, which stops the CPU at certain moments when it touches the screen memory at 3.5 MHz (see ZX Spectrum: How the Screen Is Drawn), also stretches a loop that runs in that memory, and its note comes out lower. A DMA transfer timed by its own prescaler, or the Copper, does not depend on the CPU’s speed (the DAC chapter returns to this).

A third rate, 48,000 samples a second, belongs to HDMI only: it is how the finished sum is sent over the cable, not how any sound is made. The background chapter’s section Fast enough, or it sounds wrong explains why that rate is enough.

The switches

Five registers decide which parts of the sound system are on and how they behave. An old 48K or 128K program never writes them; a Next program, or NextZXOS, sets them up. Here are the audio bits, coloured by the source each one belongs to:

  • The Peripheral 2 Setting register, NextReg $06: bit 6 sends the beeper only to the internal speaker (as Where the sound goes explains). Bits 1–0 are the AY chips’ mode: 00 YM2149, 01 AY-3-8910, and 11 holds all three chips silent in reset. The register list also names a mode 10, but the chips use only bit 0, so 10 behaves as YM2149.
  • The Peripheral 3 Setting register, NextReg $08: bit 5 chooses how each chip’s three channels are spread over the two sides (ABC or ACB), bit 4 switches the internal speaker on, bit 3 the DACs, bit 1 TurboSound (with it off, only the selected chip plays, as on a 128K), and bit 0 the issue 2 keyboard, which changes what port $FE reads back from the MIC bit.
  • The Peripheral 4 Setting register, NextReg $09: bits 7–5 put AY chips 2, 1 and 0 in mono, bit 2 silences HDMI audio.
  • NextReg $84, one byte of the four Internal Port Decoding Enables registers, NextRegs $82–$85: bit 0 enables the AY’s ports, bits 1–7 the seven families of DAC ports, from Soundrive to Specdrum. Some of those ports collide with other devices (a joystick, the mouse); these bits decide who answers.
  • The PI I2S Audio Control register, NextReg $A2: bits 7–6 switch the Pi’s audio on (left, right or both), bit 4 sets which way the data travels on its two pins, bits 3–2 mute each side, and bit 0 sends the Pi’s stream to the tape input.

After power-on, the AY chips are in YM mode with TurboSound off, the internal speaker is on, the DACs are off and held at $80, every port family is enabled, HDMI audio plays and the Pi’s audio is off. In other words, a machine that sounds exactly like a 128K until something asks for more. Sneaky, and very polite.

The chapters that follow

Each source gets a chapter of its own. The Beeper: EAR, MIC and the Tape covers port $FE, the tape input, the speaker-only beeper, and music from one bit. One AY Chip: Tones, Noise and Envelopes takes the tone counters, the noise, the envelope and the volume tables apart, and sets the AY against the YM. Then TurboSound: Three AY Chips Behind Two Ports puts three chips behind two ports, with panning, ABC, ACB and mono. The 8-Bit DACs: Four Channels, Six Sound Cards covers the six sound cards on four channels, the port families and feeding samples on time, and Audio from the Raspberry Pi: Samples on Four Wires the I2S link in both directions and the tape input from the Pi.

You can read those source chapters in any order. The Mixer: One Sum, Three Outputs comes after them, since it adds up their levels: the sum in full, the jack, the speaker and HDMI. And the last chapter, From the Machine to Your Speakers: Sound in an Emulator, is mostly about Klive itself: how an emulator turns all this into 48,000 samples a second.

How Klive does it

Klive’s Next core is a C program compiled to WebAssembly, written to behave like the hardware (see The ZX Spectrum Next Core and the FPGA). Its sound follows the hardware’s plan source by source.

Each source is a device of its own that keeps the same state as the hardware: the beeper the EAR and MIC bits and the moments they changed, the AY chips their registers and counters, stepped by the 1.75 MHz clock, the DACs their four channels and the port decoding, the Pi receiver the words latched from the link. The Pi itself is not emulated. In its place, a sample source (a WAV file or a tone, set with the pi-audio command) feeds samples into the Next’s receiving half of the link, frame by frame.

The hardware’s mixer adds its inputs continuously. Klive adds them only at the moments it needs a sample: while a frame runs, every 28,000,000 ÷ 48,000 ≈ 583 master clocks at the usual rate of 48,000 samples a second, it asks each source for its level at that moment, adds them as the mixer does, and stores the result. The frame’s samples go to the host’s sound card, which plays them while the next frame runs. The last chapter, From the Machine to Your Speakers: Sound in an Emulator, follows that path, and what happens to it at a breakpoint.

Klive’s sum keeps the hardware’s proportions, but not its zero:

  • The DACs and the Pi are taken about their rest levels ($80, 512), so a silent DAC adds 0 rather than 1,024.
  • The beeper’s EAR and MIC pass through a filter that removes their constant level, as the capacitor after the hardware’s converters does.
  • The AY chips stay as they are, 0 upwards.
  • The sum is scaled to a signed 16-bit sample, the form a sound card takes, by a factor that gives it the jack’s room above silence (the mixer chapter’s How Klive does it).

You hear the same thing. A waveform drawn from Klive’s samples, though, sits at a different level than one measured on the hardware, which is why the captures in the sound chapters are drawn about their middle.

Klive makes one stream for your computer’s speakers, so it plays one of the Next’s outputs: the audio jack, the internal speaker or HDMI, chosen under Machine › Sound › Output (the jack unless you choose otherwise), each built as on the hardware (the mixer chapter’s three outputs). A tape in Klive’s deck reaches the MIC line through the Next’s own EAR input stage, so you hear a loading tape as on the real machine. If you want to read the code yourself, it is all in src/emu/machines/zxNext/wasm/zxnext/:

WhatWhere
The beeper: EAR and MIC, and the moments they changedzxnext-beeper.c
The three AY chips, TurboSound’s selection and stereo modeszxnext-psg.c
The four DACs, their port decoding and the NextReg mirrorszxnext-dac.c
The Pi’s audio: the receiving half of the I2S linkzxnext-pi-i2s.c (the sample source: src/emu/machines/zxNext/piI2s/)
The tape: the deck, fast load, SAVE capture and the EAR input stagezxnext-tape.c (the player is the Spectrum cores’ src/emu/machines/zxSpectrum/wasm/common/zx-spectrum-tape.c)
The sum, its scaling and the samplingzxnext-audio-mixer.c

What to take home

So, what have we got? The Next keeps the 48K’s beeper, port $FE bit 4 (EAR) and bit 3 (MIC), and the 128K’s AY chip, and adds two more AY chips (TurboSound Next), four 8-bit DACs and the Raspberry Pi’s audio over an I2S link: four kinds of source. The MIC line also carries the tape input, so you hear a loading tape, and it drives the MIC socket for saving.

The sources come in two kinds. Generators, the AY chips, play by themselves once set up; level writers, the beeper and the DACs, need a write for every step. That difference decides what a sound costs the CPU, and it is why AY music with DAC drums on top is such a good match.

One mixer adds every source on a left and a right side: EAR 512, MIC 128, the AY chips up to 2,295, the DACs up to 2,040 and the Pi up to 1,023 units. The sum, at most 5,998, fits its 13-bit range of 8,191; the jack takes its lowest 12 bits, up to 4,095. And silence is 1,536, not zero. The sums leave through the audio jack and the internal speaker, both one-bit converters at 28 MHz, through HDMI at 48,000 samples a second, and to the Pi.

The AY chips run from a fixed 1.75 MHz, while the beeper’s and the DACs’ timing is the program’s, so it changes with the CPU’s speed. NextRegs $06, $08, $09, $84 and $A2 switch the parts on and off, and after power-on the Next sounds just like a 128K. Klive emulates each source in its own file and adds them at the moments it takes a sample, with the hardware’s proportions, centred and scaled to 16 bits, into one stream. Now go and meet the cast one by one.
